comment: One receiver profile per occupied apartment. This is authored social history, not a random prop scatter. Existing specialist radios in 3B, 5B and 6C remain additional sets.

crosley_pup.title: Crosley 'Pup' radio receiver
crosley_pup.documented: Small American regenerative receiver using one UV-201A tube, with exposed controls and binding posts for phones, aerial, ground and battery leads.

atwater_kent_44.title: Atwater Kent Model 44 radio receiver
atwater_kent_44.documented: American AC-operated metal-cased TRF receiver, 21.5 inches wide, with belt-linked tuning capacitors; original price $108.

marconiphone_v2.title: Marconiphone V2 broadcast receiver
marconiphone_v2.documented: Mahogany, glass, nickel, Bakelite and ebonite receiver; first heard through headphones, with a later amplifier permitting a loudspeaker.

crystal_set.title: Crystal radio receiver
crystal_set.documented: Compact passive receiver in metal and early plastic; the cited museum example measures 175 by 193 by 127 mm.

radiola_table.title: Ideal table for Radiola 18
radiola_table.documented: New York trade advertisement offers a 12 by 30 inch dedicated Radiola 18 table fitted with a magnetic or dynamic speaker.

cone_speaker.title: Mullard Pure Music cone loudspeaker
cone_speaker.documented: A free-standing 1928 cone loudspeaker, representing the separate-speaker silhouette used with receivers before integrated cabinets became universal.
